reason: IceCube's design as a cubic-kilometer South Pole telescope using Earth as a particle filter is documented across multiple institutional and scientific sources.
story: Most telescopes look up at the night sky, but the world's strangest observatory looks straight down through the center of the Earth. Buried deep beneath the South Pole, the IceCube Neutrino Observatory transformed a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice into a giant particle detector. Between 2004 and 2010, researchers used hot-water drills to melt shafts nearly two and a half kilometers deep, freezing 86 vertical cables bearing over 5,000 spherical optical sensors directly into the glacier. IceCube hunts high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, nearly massless 'ghost particles' that sail through ordinary matter. Because downward-raining cosmic rays swamp detector signals by a factor of a million, IceCube uses the solid mass of Earth as a physical shield, detecting upward-moving particles spawned by neutrinos that passed completely through the planet. In 2017, IceCube made history by tracing a single high-energy neutrino back to a supermassive black hole 3.7 billion light-years away.
angle: To look deep into space without blinding interference, astronomers built a telescope out of a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice that points straight down, using the entire planet as a physical shield.

claims.claim: The IceCube Neutrino Observatory is constructed in the Antarctic ice beneath the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station.
IceCube instruments a volume of one cubic kilometer of clear Antarctic ice.
Construction of IceCube's primary 86-string detector array was completed in December 2010.
The observatory features 86 vertical strings of photodetectors frozen into the glacier.
IceCube sensor strings reach depths between roughly 1,450 and 2,500 meters below the surface of the ice.
The spherical optical sensors embedded along the strings are known as Digital Optical Modules (DOMs).
IceCube contains more than 5,000 DOMs embedded in the ice, deployed with 60 modules per string.
Holes for the sensor strings were melted into the Antarctic ice using high-pressure hot-water drills.
IceCube was developed and supervised by the University of Wisconsin–Madison.
Francis Halzen served as the principal investigator of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory project.
Francis Halzen was awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his contributions to IceCube and the discovery of astrophysical high-energy neutrinos.
The AMANDA array preceded IceCube at the South Pole and served as its proof-of-concept.
Secondary charged particles generated by neutrino collisions in the ice travel faster than light in ice, emitting blue Cherenkov radiation.
Cosmic-ray muons traveling downward from the atmosphere above outnumber neutrino-induced muons by roughly one million to one.
IceCube searches for upward-traveling particles produced by neutrinos that passed through the Earth to filter out overhead atmospheric noise.
In September 2017, IceCube detected a high-energy neutrino that was traced back to the blazar TXS 0506+056.
The blazar TXS 0506+056 is located roughly 3.7 billion light-years from Earth.
The 2017 blazar detection was the first time a neutrino detector was used to pinpoint the location of a specific astronomical object in space.
Data from NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope helped confirm the flaring blazar origin of the 2017 neutrino.
Machine learning convolutional neural networks analyzing archival IceCube data identified seven candidate astrophysical tau neutrino events.
Unlike cosmic rays, which are deflected by galactic magnetic fields, neutrinos carry no electrical charge and travel in straight lines from their sources.
IceCube operates an automated real-time alert system to notify astronomers worldwide when high-energy astrophysical neutrino candidates are observed.

disputed: Final string deployment completion date: S7 and S1 (lead section) record December 18, 2010, while S1 (construction section) records December 17, 2010, and S2 lists simply December 2010; scripts should state 'completed in December 2010'.
Total project cost: S1 cites $279 million while S3 states $271 million; scripts should omit the exact figure or attribute as 'around 270 to 280 million dollars'.
